title: SMTP vs Email API for WordPress: SendGrid, Mailgun, Postmark, SES and Resend
description: SMTP or email API for WordPress? Compare SendGrid, Mailgun, Postmark, Amazon SES and Resend on setup, credentials and common pitfalls to pick the right one.
answer: Use an email API when you can: it sends over HTTPS, avoids blocked SMTP ports and returns clear per-message errors. Use SMTP when your provider only offers it or you want a universal option. For WordPress, Postmark, SendGrid, Mailgun, Amazon SES and Resend all work well. The right pick depends on your volume, region and budget.

blocks.x: Every email delivery plugin ultimately connects to a provider in one of two ways: SMTP or an HTTP API. The choice affects reliability, error visibility and how hard setup is.
SMTP vs email API in plain terms

head: SMTP
Email API
rows: Mail protocol over a port such as 587 or 465

blocks.x: Five providers, what each needs

head: Provider
What you enter
Watch out for
rows: API key with Mail Send permission
A successful send returns HTTP 202, not 200
Choose the US or EU region your domain is in
Some failures come back as HTTP 200 with an ErrorCode
AWS region, SMTP username and password
Use SES SMTP credentials, not AWS access keys, and match the verified region

blocks.x: VuloMail handles these quirks for you. For Postmark it checks the ErrorCode, for Vonage SMS it reads the per-message status, and for Mailgun it validates the domain before building a request URL. All 22 email APIs and 18 SMTP presets are on the [providers page](/providers).
How to pick

items: **Want a focused transactional service:** Postmark or Resend.
**Already live on AWS and want low per-message cost at scale:** Amazon SES, accepting more setup work.
**Want a well-known all-rounder:** SendGrid or Mailgun.
**Only have a mailbox:** use a [Gmail or Microsoft 365 preset](/blog/gmail-smtp-wordpress-app-password) for low volume.

blocks.title: Check current pricing yourself
blocks.x: Plans and free allowances change often, so compare the providers' own pricing pages before you commit. The plugin you pick should not lock you to one.
Set it up in five steps

items: Create the provider account and verify your sending domain.
Add the provider's SPF and DKIM records ([guide](/blog/spf-dkim-dmarc-wordpress-email-deliverability)).
Create an API key or SMTP credentials with send-only permission.
Add it as a connection in your email plugin and send a test.
Add a second provider as a backup.

blocks.x: Why your plugin choice matters

The provider moves the mail. The plugin decides what you can see and do when it goes wrong. Look for a log, a backup connection, failure alerts, encrypted credentials and support for the provider you already use. Several plugins keep those behind paid plans, while VuloMail includes them free. Compare options in our [best SMTP plugin roundup](/blog/best-wordpress-smtp-plugin).
Whichever you choose, use your own account. VuloMail sends only to providers you connect and never routes mail through a VuloLabs server.
Common mistakes when connecting a provider

items: **Using AWS access keys for Amazon SES SMTP.** SES SMTP needs its own credentials from the SES console.
**Picking the wrong region.** Mailgun, SparkPost and SES each tie your account to a region, and a mismatch returns authentication errors.
**Skipping domain verification.** Providers reject mail from unverified domains.
**Giving the key too much power.** Create a key limited to sending, not full account access.
**Assuming an API response of 200 means success.** Some providers return 200 with an error inside, so your plugin must read the body.

blocks.x: A plugin that normalises these differences saves you from learning each provider's quirks the hard way.
The short version

Pick a provider you trust, authenticate your domain, connect it through the simplest method it offers, and add a second provider as a backup. Then check the log after the first week. If a provider's first-week failure rate looks wrong, you will see it immediately and can switch without touching your site's code.

faqs.q: Is an email API better than SMTP for WordPress?
faqs.a: Usually. APIs avoid blocked ports and return clearer errors. SMTP remains a good universal option, especially for mailboxes.

faqs.q: Which email service is best for WordPress?
faqs.a: Postmark and Resend are popular for clean transactional delivery, Amazon SES for scale, and SendGrid and Mailgun as all-rounders. Compare current pricing.

faqs.q: Do I need a domain to send through these providers?
faqs.a: Yes. Verify a sending domain you own and add SPF and DKIM records so your mail is authenticated.

faqs.q: Can I use more than one provider?
faqs.a: Yes. Use one as primary and another as a backup so an outage does not stop your email.

title: Send WordPress Email With Gmail or Microsoft 365 SMTP (and When Not To)
description: Set up Gmail, Google Workspace or Microsoft 365 SMTP in WordPress with an app password, and learn the limits that make an email API a better choice.
answer: To send WordPress email through Gmail, Google Workspace or Microsoft 365, turn on two-step verification, create an app password, then enter your address and that password in an SMTP plugin's Gmail or Microsoft preset. It suits low-volume sites. Higher-volume or e-commerce sites are better served by a transactional email API.

blocks.x: Using the mailbox you already pay for is the quickest way to get WordPress email working. It is also the setup that most often breaks, because normal passwords no longer work for SMTP. Here is how to do it right and when to choose something else.
Why your normal password fails

Google, Microsoft, Yahoo and iCloud block ordinary passwords for SMTP when two-step verification is on. They want an **app password**: a separate, revocable password made just for one app. Entering your normal password is the number one cause of "authentication failed" errors.
Set up Gmail or Google Workspace

items: Turn on 2-Step Verification for the Google account.
Create an app password in your Google account's security settings and copy it.
In VuloMail, add a connection and pick the **Gmail** or **Google Workspace** preset.
Enter the full address and paste the app password.
Set the From address to the same mailbox, then send a test.

blocks.x: Set up Microsoft 365 or Outlook.com

items: If multi-factor authentication is on, create an app password. For Outlook.com, use Advanced security options → App passwords.
For Microsoft 365, ask your admin to allow app passwords and SMTP AUTH. Without that, sign-in fails.
Pick the **Microsoft 365** or **Outlook.com** preset in VuloMail and enter your address and password.
Send a test email.

blocks.title: Other mailbox presets
blocks.x: VuloMail also has one-click presets for Zoho Mail, Yahoo, iCloud, AOL, Yandex, Fastmail, Titan, Purelymail, Migadu, Namecheap Private Email and Rackspace. Most need an app password too.
The limits you should know

head: Limit
What it means for your site
rows: Personal Gmail allows roughly 500 messages a day and Workspace roughly 2,000. Check Google's current limits
From address locked to the mailbox
Sending as another address often gets rewritten or rejected
No bounce webhooks or per-message delivery dashboards
Your mailbox mixes human and automated mail
The app password sits on your site, so revoke it if the site is ever compromised

blocks.x: When to use an email API instead

items: You run WooCommerce or send more than a few hundred messages a day.
You want delivery and bounce reporting per message.
You want to keep sending separate from your team's inbox.

blocks.x: Services such as Postmark, SendGrid, Amazon SES or Resend are built for this. Our [SMTP vs email API guide](/blog/smtp-vs-email-api-wordpress) explains the trade-offs, and the [providers page](/providers) shows what each one needs.
Make Gmail a backup, not the only route

A mailbox preset is a handy second connection. Set an API provider as primary and Gmail as the backup, and an outage on either side no longer stops your site. See the [failover guide](/blog/wordpress-email-failover-backup-smtp) for the setup.

VuloMail stores your app password encrypted with libsodium, masks it after saving and sends it only to the provider it belongs to. If a connection suddenly reads "Incomplete" after a site migration, your wp-config security keys changed, so re-enter the password.
Troubleshooting checklist

items: **Authentication failed:** you used a normal password. Create an app password.
**App password option missing:** 2-Step Verification is off, or an admin has disabled app passwords.
**Microsoft 365 sign-in refused:** SMTP AUTH is disabled for the mailbox. Ask your admin to enable it.
**Emails sent but in spam:** add SPF, DKIM and DMARC for your domain. See our [deliverability guide](/blog/spf-dkim-dmarc-wordpress-email-deliverability).
**Worked, then stopped:** the app password was revoked, or the account hit its daily cap.

blocks.x: Yandex app passwords can take two to three hours to become active, so wait before assuming a new one is wrong.
Your next step

If you are starting from scratch, set up the mailbox preset today to get email flowing, then plan a move to a transactional provider before traffic grows. Because VuloMail lets you hold several connections, you can add the new provider as primary without removing the mailbox, and keep it as your safety net.

faqs.q: Can I use Gmail SMTP with WordPress?
faqs.a: Yes. Turn on 2-Step Verification, create an app password and use it in a Gmail preset or SMTP settings. It suits low-volume sites.

faqs.q: Why does Gmail SMTP say authentication failed?
faqs.a: You probably used your normal password. Gmail needs an app password when 2-Step Verification is on.

faqs.q: Is Gmail SMTP good enough for WooCommerce?
faqs.a: For a very small store, perhaps. Daily caps and no delivery reporting make a transactional email API the safer choice.

faqs.q: Does VuloMail support Google sign-in?
faqs.a: No. Its Gmail preset uses an app password. Some other plugins offer Google sign-in.

title: WordPress Email Log: How to Track, Search and Resend Every Email
description: Track every WordPress email with a delivery log. Learn what to record, how to search and resend failed messages, and how to keep the log private.
answer: A WordPress email log records every message your site sends, with its recipient, subject, status, provider and any error. Use it to confirm delivery, debug failures and resend messages. Choose a logger that stores bodies only if you opt in, masks recipients and prunes old entries.

blocks.x: "Did the customer get that email?" is the most common support question a WordPress site owner faces, and without a log the honest answer is "no idea." An email log turns that guess into a lookup.
What a good email log records

head: Field
Why it matters
rows: Match a send to a customer's complaint
Know whether the primary or the backup delivered it
Look up inbox placement in your provider's dashboard

blocks.x: What "Sent" does and does not mean

This is the part most people get wrong. A "Sent" status means your provider accepted the message. It does not prove the inbox received it. Delivery, bounces and spam placement are reported in your provider's dashboard, and you find the message there using the Provider ID stored in the log entry.

blocks.title: Rule of thumb
blocks.x: Log tells you WordPress and the provider did their part. The provider dashboard tells you what the receiving mailbox did.
Search, filter and resend

items: Open the log and filter by status to see failures first.
Search by recipient or subject to find a specific message.
Open the entry to read the error, such as an HTTP 401 from SendGrid, which points to a bad API key.
Fix the cause, then resend from the log.

blocks.x: Resending requires the message content to have been stored, which is why VuloMail makes content storage an opt-in setting. Turn it on only if you need resend, since stored bodies can contain personal data.
Keep the log private
An email log is a record of your customers' messages, which makes it sensitive. Look for these controls:

items: **Message bodies off by default,** stored only if you choose.
**Recipient masking,** so addresses are partly hidden in the admin.
**Automatic pruning** of old entries so data does not pile up.
**No outside copy.** The log should stay in your own database.

blocks.x: VuloMail's log stays on your site, never leaves it, and has no tracking. See the [security page](/security) for the encryption and privacy details. Check your own privacy obligations, since what you may keep depends on your jurisdiction.
One log for email and SMS

VuloMail keeps email and SMS in one log, with one row per message even when failover was used. A row shows the primary attempt, the backup and the last resort together, rather than scattering them across several lines.
Free versus paid logs

Many popular plugins gate the log. WP Mail SMTP's log and resend are Pro features from $99 a year at full price, and the full log is paid in Easy WP SMTP and GoSMTP too. FluentSMTP, Post SMTP, SureMail and VuloMail include a log free. The [full comparison](/blog/best-wordpress-smtp-plugin) has the details.
Pair your log with [failure alerts](/blog/wordpress-email-failover-backup-smtp) so you learn about a problem from the dashboard, not from a customer.
When a log saves you hours

items: **A customer says they never got a receipt.** Search their address and see the send, the status and the provider ID.
**Password resets stop working.** Filter by failed and read the error. An expired key shows up immediately.
**A form plugin goes quiet.** If nothing from it appears in the log, it bypasses wp_mail() and needs its own mail settings.
**You switch providers.** Compare the failure rate before and after the move.

blocks.x: Set it up in two minutes

Install the plugin, add a connection, send a test and open the log to confirm the entry appears. Decide whether you need resend. If you do, switch on content storage and set a retention period so old messages are pruned automatically. If you do not, leave bodies off and keep only the metadata, which is enough to answer most delivery questions.

faqs.q: How do I see emails sent from WordPress?
faqs.a: Install an email plugin with a delivery log. It records every message that passes through wp_mail(), with status, recipient and errors.

faqs.q: Can I resend a failed WordPress email?
faqs.a: Yes, if the plugin stored the message content. In VuloMail, turn on message-content storage, then resend from the log entry.

faqs.q: Does the email log store message bodies?
faqs.a: Not in VuloMail unless you opt in. That keeps customer content out of your database by default.

faqs.q: Does 'Sent' mean the email was delivered?
faqs.a: No. It means the provider accepted it. Check the provider's dashboard with the Provider ID for delivery status.

title: WooCommerce Emails Not Sending or Going to Spam? A Store Owner's Fix List
description: WooCommerce order emails not sending or landing in spam? Fix missing receipts, failed-order alerts and password resets with SMTP, DNS records and a delivery log.
keywords: WooCommerce new order email not received
answer: WooCommerce emails fail for the same reason other WordPress emails do: they leave through unauthenticated PHP mail. Connect an SMTP or email-API provider, send from an address on your own domain, publish SPF, DKIM and DMARC records, and keep a delivery log so a missing order receipt is never a mystery.

blocks.x: A missing order confirmation costs real money. Customers email support, open disputes or assume the store is a scam. WooCommerce sends all its emails through WordPress's standard `wp_mail()` function, so the fix lives at the WordPress level, not in WooCommerce settings.
Which WooCommerce emails are at risk?

head: Email
Sent to
Cost of losing it
rows: You miss a sale to ship

blocks.x: Why they go missing

items: **Host mail is unauthenticated.** Receivers distrust it, so order emails land in spam.
**The From address doesn't match your domain.** WooCommerce defaults to an address based on your site. Set one on your domain and verify it with your provider.
**Provider limits.** A flash sale can exceed a free plan's daily cap.
**A plugin bypassing `wp_mail()`.** Some marketing plugins send directly, so your SMTP plugin never touches those messages.
**Spam-folder routing for the admin address.** Your own new-order email lands in spam because it is sent from and to the same domain.

blocks.x: The fix list, in order

items: Install an email delivery plugin and connect a transactional provider such as Postmark, SendGrid, Amazon SES or Resend. Our [providers page](/providers) lists what each needs.
Set WooCommerce's From name and address to a real mailbox on your domain.
Add SPF, DKIM and DMARC records ([how-to here](/blog/spf-dkim-dmarc-wordpress-email-deliverability)).
Place a test order and confirm the customer and admin emails both arrive in the inbox.
Add a backup connection on a second provider.
Turn on failure alerts so a broken connection reaches you by text, not by a customer complaint.

blocks.title: Prove an email was sent
blocks.x: When a customer says they never got their receipt, the delivery log settles it. It shows when WooCommerce sent the message, which provider accepted it and the provider's message ID so you can check inbox placement there.
Add SMS so a missed email does not mean a missed update

Even healthy email gets filtered. Texting the customer when an order is confirmed, completed or refunded gives them a second channel. VuloMail has six customer alerts and eight store alerts for WooCommerce; see our [WooCommerce SMS guide](/blog/woocommerce-sms-notifications).
Choose a plugin that fits a store

For a store, three features matter more than anything else: a log, a backup connection and failure alerts. Several popular plugins reserve those for paid plans, which adds a yearly cost per store. VuloMail includes all three for free, along with the WooCommerce SMS alerts, with no Pro edition.

One honest limit: VuloMail does not track opens or clicks, so if marketing analytics matter, pair it with a dedicated email service. Use our [comparison page](/compare) to see where each plugin stands.
A quick weekly habit

items: Skim the log for failed sends.
Re-run the DNS check after any hosting or domain change.
Send a test order after plugin updates.

blocks.x: Test your store the way a customer would

Open a private browser window and place a real low-value order, or use a free product. Check three inboxes: the customer's, your admin address and one on a different provider such as Gmail. If any lands in spam or never arrives, open the delivery log for that message before changing anything. The log tells you whether the problem is at WordPress, the provider or the receiving mailbox, which saves hours of guessing.
Your next step

Do the test order today, before your next campaign or sale. A store that discovers its email problem during a promotion loses both the sales and the trust. A store that finds it on a quiet Tuesday loses nothing. Start with the [setup guide](/get-started), connect a provider and run the five-minute check.

title: SPF, DKIM and DMARC for WordPress: Fix Emails Going to Spam
description: WordPress emails landing in spam? Learn what SPF, DKIM and DMARC records do, see copy-ready examples, and check them for your sending domain in minutes.
answer: WordPress emails go to spam when your domain can't prove it authorised the sending server. SPF lists allowed servers, DKIM adds a cryptographic signature, and DMARC tells inboxes what to do when either fails. Publish all three as DNS records for your sending domain, then send from an address on that domain.

blocks.x: If your contact form notifications and order emails keep landing in spam, the content is rarely the problem. Mailbox providers decide mostly on one question: can this domain prove it sent this message? Three DNS records answer it.
What SPF, DKIM and DMARC actually do

head: Record
What it does
Where it lives
rows: Lists the servers allowed to send for your domain
A TXT record on your domain
Signs each message so receivers can verify it was not altered
A TXT or CNAME record your provider gives you
Tells receivers what to do if SPF or DKIM fails, and sends you reports

blocks.x: Since 2024, Google and Yahoo have required authentication from bulk senders, and in practice every site now benefits from having all three in place.
Copy-ready examples

example.com.   TXT   "v=spf1 include:_spf.example-provider.com ~all"
_dmarc.example.com.   TXT   "v=DMARC1; p=none; rua=mailto:reports@example.com"
blocks.title: DNS records (replace with your provider's values)

blocks.x: Your email provider shows the exact SPF include and DKIM records to add. Never copy another site's values.

items: **One SPF record only.** Two SPF records break SPF. Combine all senders into one.
**Mind the lookup limit.** SPF allows 10 DNS lookups. Too many `include:` entries fail silently.
**Start DMARC at `p=none`.** Read the reports first, then move to `quarantine` and `reject`.

blocks.x: The five-step fix

items: Pick a sending domain you own and use it as the From address, not a free Gmail or Yahoo address.
Add your provider's SPF and DKIM records at your DNS host.
Add a DMARC record starting at `p=none` with a reporting address.
Run a DNS check from your WordPress dashboard.
Send a test and open the message headers to confirm SPF, DKIM and DMARC all show **pass**.

blocks.title: Check from your own site
blocks.x: VuloMail's Tools → Diagnostics page includes a sender-domain DNS check for SPF and DMARC that runs from your own server, so your domain is not sent to an outside service. DKIM lives in your provider's dashboard, so confirm it there.
Other reasons emails reach spam

items: **A From address that doesn't match your sending domain.** Mismatch fails DMARC alignment.
**A shared or low-reputation IP.** Cheap hosts mail from shared IPs. A dedicated provider connection avoids that.
**Sending through PHP mail.** Unauthenticated messages are suspect by default.
**Spammy content.** All-image emails, URL shorteners and misleading subjects all hurt.

blocks.x: Moving from PHP mail to an authenticated provider is usually the single biggest improvement. See our guide to [WordPress not sending emails](/blog/wordpress-not-sending-emails) for the full list.
Keep watching after setup

Deliverability drifts. DNS records get edited, providers change, and a plugin update can change the sender. Review your DMARC reports, re-run diagnostics after any change, and keep a [backup connection](/blog/wordpress-email-failover-backup-smtp) so a reputation problem on one provider does not stop all mail.
Remember that "Sent" in your log means a provider accepted the message. Inbox placement is shown in your provider's own dashboard, where you can look up the message by its provider ID.
Read a message header to confirm it works

After you publish your records, send a test to a Gmail address, open the message and choose **Show original**. Gmail displays three lines, one each for SPF, DKIM and DMARC. You want to see **PASS** on all three.

items: **SPF fail or softfail:** the sending server is missing from your SPF record.
**DKIM none:** the DKIM record was not published, or your provider is not signing yet.
**DMARC fail:** SPF or DKIM passed for a different domain than your From address. Align them.

blocks.x: Fix the first failing line, wait for DNS to update, and test again. Change one thing at a time so you know which edit worked.

faqs.q: Why do my WordPress emails go to spam?
faqs.a: Usually because the domain lacks SPF, DKIM or DMARC records, the From address doesn't match the sending domain, or the site sends through unauthenticated PHP mail.

faqs.q: Do I need all three of SPF, DKIM and DMARC?
faqs.a: Yes. They work together, and major inboxes expect all three, especially for higher-volume senders.

faqs.q: Can a WordPress plugin fix my DNS records?
faqs.a: A plugin can check them and tell you what is missing. You still add the records at your DNS host.

faqs.q: How long do DNS changes take?
faqs.a: Often minutes, but allow up to 48 hours for changes to propagate everywhere.

title: WordPress Email Failover: How to Set Up a Backup SMTP Connection
description: Set up WordPress email failover with a backup SMTP or API connection so password resets and order emails still send when your main provider goes down.
answer: WordPress email failover means configuring a second sending connection that takes over automatically when your primary provider rejects or can't send a message. Choose a backup on a different provider, set it as the fallback in your SMTP plugin, then test by deliberately breaking the primary key.

blocks.x: Your site depends on email more than it seems to. Password resets, order confirmations, booking notices and admin alerts all flow through one provider account. If that account is suspended, rate-limited or simply having a bad afternoon, those messages stop, and nobody tells you.
What is email failover?

Failover is a standby sending route. Your plugin tries the primary connection first. If the primary reports a failure, it tries the backup. A third tier hands the message to WordPress's own mailer as a last resort. The visitor never notices, and you still see what happened.

head: Tier
What it is
When it runs
rows: Your main provider, such as SendGrid or Postmark
A second provider or SMTP account
When the primary reports a failure

blocks.x: Why a single provider is a risk

items: **Outages.** Even the biggest providers have incidents.
**Account holds.** A billing lapse or a spam flag can pause sending without warning.
**Expired credentials.** API keys get rotated or revoked.
**Limits.** Free and entry plans cap daily volume, and sales spikes hit those caps.

blocks.x: A backup does not need to be expensive. A free-tier account on a second provider is enough to keep password resets and order emails moving.
How to choose a backup provider

items: **Use a different company from your primary.** Two accounts at one vendor share the same outage.
**Match the sending domain.** Add the backup's SPF and DKIM records so mail from your domain still passes authentication.
**Prefer simple setup.** A Gmail or Microsoft 365 SMTP preset works, though daily limits are lower than a transactional provider.
**Verify the From address** on both accounts, because a rejected sender looks like a failed send.

Add your primary connection: any SMTP server, one of 22 email APIs or a preset.

Watch the duplicate-email edge case

The backup runs only after the primary reports a failure, so customers normally get one copy. In the rare case where a provider accepts a message but still reports an error, the backup would send it again. That trade-off is why it is better to risk a duplicate than to lose a password reset.
Get alerted when failover happens

A backup that quietly saves you can also hide a broken primary for weeks. VuloMail records every attempt on a single log row, so you can see which connection delivered, and it can text you when an email fails to send. Alerts are limited to one text every 15 minutes, so an outage does not flood your phone.

A realistic failover example

Imagine a store with Postmark as primary and a Google Workspace SMTP preset as backup. One morning Postmark rejects every request because a billing card expired. Without failover, order receipts stop and nobody notices until customers complain. With failover, each message fails once at Postmark, succeeds through the backup, and the log shows exactly when the primary started failing. You fix the card the same day instead of finding out next week.

title: WordPress Not Sending Emails? 8 Causes and How to Fix Each One
description: WordPress not sending emails? Find the real cause (PHP mail, blocked ports, missing SPF/DKIM, plugin conflicts) and fix it with a step-by-step checklist.
answer: WordPress usually fails to send email because it hands messages to your web host's basic PHP mail function, which hosts throttle or block and inboxes distrust. The fix is to send through an authenticated SMTP or email-API connection, add SPF, DKIM and DMARC records for your domain, and keep a log so every failure is visible.

blocks.x: When WordPress stops sending email, password resets, order receipts and contact-form messages all disappear at once, and you usually find out from an unhappy customer. The cause is rarely WordPress itself. It is almost always how the message leaves your server.
Why WordPress emails fail in the first place

Every email WordPress creates goes through one function, `wp_mail()`. Out of the box, that function passes the message to PHP's `mail()`, which asks your web server to deliver it with no login and no proof that your site owns the sender address. Receiving servers treat that as suspicious, and many hosts disable or rate-limit it to stop spam.
Fixing it means giving WordPress a proper, authenticated route out. That is what an SMTP plugin or email-API connector does.
The 8 most common causes, with fixes

items: **Your host blocks PHP mail.** Many shared hosts switch it off. Fix: send through SMTP or an email API instead.
**The message is sent but lands in spam.** The domain has no SPF, DKIM or DMARC record. Fix: add all three (see our [SPF, DKIM and DMARC guide](/blog/spf-dkim-dmarc-wordpress-email-deliverability)).
**A mismatched From address.** Sending as `you@gmail.com` from a different server fails authentication. Fix: use an address on your own domain that your provider has verified.
**Wrong SMTP port or encryption.** Port 25 is commonly blocked. Fix: use 587 with STARTTLS or 465 with SSL.
**Bad credentials.** Gmail, Yahoo, iCloud and others need an app password, not your normal one. Fix: generate an app password.
**Two email plugins fighting.** Both try to deliver the same message. Fix: keep one and deactivate the other.
**A plugin that bypasses `wp_mail()`.** It talks to an email service directly, so your SMTP plugin never sees it. Fix: check that plugin's own mail settings.
**A provider rejection you never see.** The provider refuses the message and nothing records it. Fix: use a plugin with a delivery log and failure alerts.
